stops.name: Corsica, Ponte Novu, the fall of Paoli
stops.campa: On the bridge over the Golo at Ponte Novu the last army of free Corsica breaks under French guns. Pasquale Paoli's militia, in which Carlo Buonaparte has ridden as aide, is scattered; the general sails for exile in England within the month. Three months before his second son is born, Carlo makes his peace with the conquering crown, accepts a place among the island's new French nobility, and carries his pregnant wife Letizia, who followed the army on muleback through the mountains, home to Ajaccio. The cause is lost before the boy who will avenge and betray it draws breath.

stops.name: Ajaccio, birth in the Casa Bonaparte
stops.campa: Letizia Bonaparte, hearing mass at the cathedral of Ajaccio, is seized with labor and walks the few steps home; she gives birth, the family will say, on a sofa covered in an old tapestry of Homeric heroes, so quick was the child in coming. He is christened Napoleone, for a great-uncle, in the Casa Bonaparte on the day of the Assumption. Carlo, lawyer and gentleman of modest estate, and Letizia, nineteen and iron-willed, will raise eight children in these rooms on the fault line between old Corsica and the new French order that has just swallowed it.

stops.name: Brienne-le-Château, the military school
stops.campa: A gaunt, friendless Corsican boy of nine arrives at the Royal Military School of Brienne, one of twelve founded by Louis XVI for the sons of poor nobility. He speaks French badly, is mocked for his island accent and his given name, and withdraws into mathematics, geography, and the history of Plutarch's great captains. He excels at maps and siege-craft, is made a corporal of the model battalion the boys drill with, and dreams, his sister will remember, of leading Corsica back to Paoli's cause. Five years of ploughing through Latin buy him, at the end, a gift for guns.
stops.quote: I lived like a bear, in a little cell of my own... I looked upon my comrades with a species of indignation.
stops.quote_source: Napoleon's recollections of Brienne, recorded by Bourrienne and Las Cases

stops.name: Paris, the École Militaire, the commission
stops.campa: At the École Militaire on the Champ de Mars, in the year after his father's death leaves the family in want, the sixteen-year-old cadet sits the examinations of the artillery corps: the one branch of the service where mathematics outweighs birth. He places forty-second of fifty-eight candidates, the only Corsican in his year to pass at all, and is commissioned second lieutenant in La Fère regiment. He leaves Paris within days for the garrison at Valence, a friendless young officer with a library card, a subscription to Rousseau, and no fortune but his slide-rule.

stops.name: Ajaccio, the break with Paoli, exile of the family
stops.campa: The Revolution has split Corsica as it has split France. Paoli, restored to power and now suspect to Paris, breaks with the young officer's family when brother Lucien denounces him before the Convention; the Bonapartes are declared enemies of the Corsican cause and their house is sacked by a mob. Napoleon, his mother, and his sisters flee down to the harbor by night and take ship for Toulon with almost nothing saved. He lands in France a refugee of twenty-three, stripped of the island loyalty that shaped him, with only the Revolution left to serve.

stops.name: Toulon, the siege, the artillery command
stops.campa: At the siege of royalist, English-held Toulon the wounded chief of artillery is replaced by a twenty-four-year-old captain recommended by his fellow Corsican Saliceti. Bonaparte lays out the batteries himself, walks the guns under fire, has a horse shot from under him, and takes a bayonet wound in the thigh. His plan, to seize the promontory of L'Éguillette and drive the British fleet from the roads with converging fire, succeeds in a single night's assault; Hood's ships stand out to sea, and Toulon falls. The representatives promote him brigadier general at twenty-four, over guns pointed correctly for the first time in his life.

stops.name: Paris, 13 Vendémiaire, the guns before Saint-Roch
stops.campa: The Convention, threatened by a royalist rising of the Paris sections, hands its defense to Barras, who calls on the unemployed Corsican general idling in the capital. Bonaparte sends Murat racing for the cannon parked at the Sablons before the insurgents can seize them, and lines his guns along the rue Saint-Honoré and the steps of the church of Saint-Roch. When the columns of the sections advance he opens with grapeshot at point-blank range; the crowd breaks and scatters within minutes. The Convention is saved, the phrase 'a whiff of grapeshot' enters the language for it, and Barras remembers the name of the gunner.

stops.name: Paris, marriage to Joséphine
stops.campa: At the mairie of the second arrondissement, past ten at night, the twenty-six-year-old commander of the Army of Italy marries Rose de Beauharnais, six years his elder, widow of a guillotined vicomte, mother of two, and mistress lately of the all-powerful Barras. He signs the register giving himself an extra year and her a few less; witnesses include Barras himself. Two days later he leaves for the front without her, and begins from the road the flood of letters that will call her Joséphine: the name he has already decided suits her better than her own.
stops.quote: I awake full of you. Your image and the intoxicating pleasures of last night have left no rest to my senses... Sweet and incomparable Joséphine, what a strange effect you have upon my heart!
stops.quote_source: Napoleon to Joséphine, December 1795 – March 1796 (Correspondance de Napoléon Ier)

stops.name: Lodi, the bridge
stops.campa: At the long wooden bridge over the Adda at Lodi, Austrian guns rake the crossing at point-blank range. Bonaparte forms columns of grenadiers under the parapet, out of the line of fire, and leads the charge himself among his generals, sword in hand, into the smoke; the bridge is carried and the rear guard broken. That night, walking the field, he first feels, he will tell Bourrienne years later, the ambition of executing great things stir in him as more than a fantastic dream. His soldiers, admiring the gunner who still sights his own cannon, begin calling him le petit corporal.
stops.quote: It was not till after Lodi that I saw myself as a superior being, and conceived the ambition of performing great things which so far had filled my thoughts only as a fantastic dream.

stops.name: Arcole, the flag on the bridge
stops.campa: Against the Austrians relieving Mantua, the army stalls before the narrow causeway and bridge at Arcole, swept by artillery from the far bank. When his infantry balk, Bonaparte seizes a tricolor standard himself and runs onto the dike in the open, calling the grenadiers to follow their general; his aide Muiron falls dead at his side shielding him, and he is pulled back into the marsh, nearly drowned, by his own staff. The bridge is not taken that hour, but the image, the general with the flag under fire, outruns the fact and becomes, within the year, the Republic's most reproduced picture.
stops.quote: Grenadiers, come and seek your colour!
stops.quote_source: General Augereau at the bridge of Arcole, 15-17 November 1796; Bonaparte repeats the act with a second flag

stops.name: Campo Formio, the treaty, Venice given away
stops.campa: At the château of Campo Formio, negotiating with imperial Austria on his own authority and largely against his government's instructions, twenty-eight-year-old General Bonaparte dictates the peace of a continent. Austria cedes the Austrian Netherlands and recognizes French dominion in Italy; in exchange, Bonaparte hands over the thousand-year republic of Venice, never conquered by him and occupied only by trickery months before, as a coin of the settlement. He returns to Paris a peacemaker and a name greater than the Directory that employs him, having taught Europe that a general in the field can make its treaties.
stops.quote: The Republic of Venice has no other title than that of a conquest which I have made.
stops.quote_source: Bonaparte, letter justifying the cession of Venice, 1797 (Correspondance)

stops.name: Alexandria, the landing
stops.campa: Slipping past Nelson's fleet in fog and luck, the expedition of five hundred ships lands its army on the beach west of Alexandria. Bonaparte reads his soldiers a proclamation promising respect for Islam and the Prophet, casting the invasion as liberation from the Mamluk beys rather than conquest of Egypt; few of the exhausted, thirst-maddened troops who storm the walls that same night believe a word of it, but the words themselves, printed also in Arabic, announce a new kind of European war, fought as much with printing presses and savants as with bayonets.
stops.quote: Peoples of Egypt, you will be told that I have come to destroy your religion; do not believe it... I respect God, his Prophet, and the Qur'an more than the Mamluks do.
stops.quote_source: Bonaparte's proclamation to the Egyptians, 2 July 1798
